source_text: It occurs to me that we've basically delivered what M-points-de-fuite was asking for; it proposed a short series of other marks like ✓ which I haven't been using regularly.  I think the new system is better.

reply_text:
㊥ Gist: I agree the new marks are better. They also follow M-points-de-fuite's own rule more closely than its ✓ ✘ 💡 marks did: recognise the act first, and keep typed symbols for overrides. Of the mission's four acceptance items, the marks cover one and part of another, and two are still open. I've posted an offer for what to do with the old keys. "🈸:yes 1" records the change in the mission and unbinds C-c . and C-c , with a note of when to restore them. "🈸:yes 2" records it in the mission only.

㊢ (what the mission asked for) M-points-de-fuite (`futon2/holes/`, marked closed in June) sets three tiers:
1. Recognise the act from the turn itself. For example, mentioning a mission clocks you in.
2. Read light deterministic cues, such as "not X but Y" for a correction.
3. Type explicit symbols, but only as an override.

The ✓ ✘ 💡 hydra on C-c . sat in the third tier. Since you were the only one typing those marks, they rarely got used.

🈖 (why the new setup fits better) Each piece of what we built this week maps onto one of those tiers:
- **First and second tiers:** 象 recognises your turns, and 小象 does the same classically, with no language model.
- **Agents' side:** agents now mark their own replies, so that structure comes from them rather than from you.
- **Third tier:** you only type a mark where it does something, as in "🈸:yes 1". That records an Elephant-2000 agreement, not just a symbol in the text.

㊟ (the mission's acceptance list)
- **Partly met:** "a deterministic turn-level recognizer". 小象 is one, but it outputs intent labels, not the sorry, preference, method and proof-edge records the item names.
- **Met, for agreements:** "inline override notation". Marks with a colon on Elephant-2000 records do this.
- **Not met:** method declarations minting claim nodes and proof edges in one step, and a recorded trial of whether recognised acts lead into new work without a mission set up first.

So I'd write this down as the mission's notation being superseded, not as the whole mission being done.

🈸 (one decision) Offer `act:31e3fc8d-2436-462f-a8a1-eb470d8eeb2c`:
1. Add a dated note to M-points-de-fuite saying the reply marks supersede its marks. Unbind C-c . and C-c , but keep the commands, with a comment at the unbinding saying when to bind them again. That follows the pattern on your prompt line, WR-26: switch a capability off only with the condition for switching it back on written there.
2. Add the mission note only, and leave the old keys bound.

previous_reply_acts.author: claude-17
previous_reply_acts.text:
(what the log shows) This is futon1b's journal for the 18 seconds after your "🈸:yes 1" at 14:02:13:
- **Evidence:** your turn's evidence was written and read back in under 50 ms.
- **The slow reads:** the list of this session's offers took 6,533 ms. Then the list of agreements on an older offer of mine took 7,299 ms. Run now, both take about 0.5 ms.
- **What ran at the same time:** the reads for the pattern card shown in your prompt line, each about 2.7 s. These are queries for the state at a given moment, and the moment changes every turn, so they're never cached. Evidence writes were also going on.
- **The result:** the agreement was written at 14:02:27 by your own request. The server kept going after Emacs gave up at 3 s.

previous_reply_acts.author: claude-17
previous_reply_acts.text: (what I couldn't pin down) It isn't futon1b's limit on concurrent heavy reads: that allows 4, and at most 3 were held. I ran one uncached pattern-card read alongside an offer read, and the offer read still took 3 ms. So the slowdown needs more than one competing read, or something else that was happening at 14:02. Finding it is futon1b work: reproduce several uncached reads at once, the way a turn start does.

previous_reply_acts.author: claude-17
previous_reply_acts.text:
(the Emacs change, commits 53dbffd2, 6fdced7f, d63d2647)
- **Background request:** `agent-chat--agreement-post-async` sends the agreement in the background, with a 60 s deadline. The outcome line goes to the buffer that asked, even if you've moved to another buffer by then.
- **Clearer refusals:** a refusal now gives its reason, e.g. "http 403, evidence-not-operator-turn".
- **Agent timing:** the agent still gets the turn immediately. If the server is slow, the agent sees the agreement in the next turn's header, as happened this turn.

previous_reply_acts.author: claude-17
previous_reply_acts.text:
(what I checked)
- **Live, in your Emacs:** I fired your real yes and an agent turn's evidence at the server. The first came back 200 with agreement `act:e77e3e43…` (the existing one, not a duplicate). The second came back 403, each to its own buffer.
- **Tests:** the agent-chat ERT tests pass, 54 of 54. I had missed that they called the old synchronous request function, so I updated them. The new test checks that the turn is sent before the answer arrives and that the line lands in the right buffer. Both the updated test and the new one fail against the old blocking code.
- **Not run:** the rest of the Emacs test files.
